title: Suzuki Roshi's Students, Katherine Thanas
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads two short chapters by Katherine Thanas, a direct student of Suzuki Roshi, from her book The Truth of This Life. In "Set Ourselves to Zero," Katherine judges a bemused young man at Suzuki Roshi's ashes ceremony at Tassajara, until a thought arises that the moment is already perfect. In "No Pressure to Improve," she urges stopping the veering off and moving toward fear in small steps, breathing with it inside the body. Nomon describes a cold, dark stone of fear in the gut and the practice of naming fear while turning down the story that someone must be upset. Nomon closes by asking listeners whether greed, hatred, or delusion most often grabs them.

sentences.text: Last week we were appreciating Suzuki Roshi's teaching on Beginner's Mind that begins the teachings in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind and also sets its title.
In the talk I played with and broadened the dichotomy of Beginner's Mind and Expert's Mind a bit.
We explored a little around what happens when we get tight, self-focused, maybe a little self-righteous or fearful or something.
We can have that experience, and we can also have the experience of being more open, trusting, settled.
What seems to be involved in this shifting back and forth, and all the shades of black and brown in between?
How can we recognize our state without believing so much in the story?
Have a little wise perspective on the workings of our conditioned mind, our karma, the sprouting of the many seeds in our storehouse depending on conditions and our attitude.
And we thought a little bit about: can we shift back and forth between these states, or is it just a matter of being patient and holding on?

One of the things that's interesting about Suzuki Roshi's teachings, and most of the teachings from the early Asian teachers, is that Asian Zen teachers really didn't get too much into psychological topics like that.
Suzuki Roshi had such an amazing way of describing the territory, pointing to the path with his words.
But he doesn't really say how to walk on it exactly, or what to do.
There's not a lot in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind that feels really all that practical, or strictly speaking useful in that tool-using way that we think about: how can I change this to that?
How can I fix this or fix that?
There are some specific instructions on Zazen for sure.
That's coming right up in the book.
Although it wasn't really applicable to this book, we know that he taught very specifically about just the Zen form and the Zen way of life.
The students did all the rituals that we're doing and then some.
He also brought in some other Japanese teachers to help with that.
But he didn't talk so much about moods or thoughts or psychology.
And I think this is, in a way, frustrating: what do we do?
But also liberating, depending on how you look at it.
One of our teachers, I forget who, said the wonderful thing about Soto Zen in particular is that there's no method.
Or we could say it's a methodless method.
No step by step.
Suzuki Roshi says somewhere we don't practice stepladder Zen here so much.
If we did, we'd abandon the stepladders once we've climbed up them.
We just practice, right?
We just sit.
We just live.
We just are.
We open up to Buddha expressing through us, through our hearts, through our bodies, through our boundless, compassionate minds.

That's really helpful, I think, because we are so conditioned to try to break things down into little pieces, figure out the right steps, figure out how to do it right, measure and evaluate whether we're doing it right.
Are we making progress?
Yes, we're encouraged.
No, we're discouraged.
What if we have a way of life that steps out of that, steps beyond all that doing and figuring and sorting and solving?
And yet it's also helpful to have some advice, to have a method, to have something to focus on or take up at least for a time.
So in this series of talks on Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, it's going to take a while to go through it, because we're going to go through it really carefully.
It would take even longer because I thought I'd sprinkle in teachings from Suzuki Roshi's direct students, those who went on to become teachers themselves, and how they spoke about practice.
Many of them, their expression is indeed a lot more practical in that way.
But it's a treacherous thing, right?
Who is it that's being practical?
What is there to be practical about?
The minute we get too involved in trying to get better and improve, the whole thing narrows down and can get small.
So maybe it's a matter of getting fluid about that: sometimes small, focused, thinking that we can hold on to some conceptual understanding and work with it and use it.
We probably can, but then broadening out, opening up.
So maybe we're really lucky we have access to both ways of looking at it in these two generations of our ancestors, of our teachers.
A few of Suzuki Roshi's direct descendants are still teaching, but he died in 1971.
So what's that, 40 years ago?
So many of them are now themselves passing away.
Anyway, I wanted to share a few little teachings from Katherine Thanas tonight.
A book recently came out of her teachings called The Truth of This Life.
She joined Suzuki Roshi's Sangha a little bit later in life, when she was 39.
I won't say her whole bio, just the gist.
She was the same generation as Blanche Hartman.
I remember Blanche talking a lot, when I studied with her, about how that was a little awkward, to be late 30s or 40s with this crew of just fired-up 22-year-olds.
Just fired up, 22, 25, completely giving up everything, devoting themselves completely to the Sangha, a very fired-up situation.
So it was interesting to come into that a little more mature, a little more measured.
Like Trudy Dixon, whom we heard about last week, who was the editor and really the creator of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Katherine was quite well educated.
She went to prestigious universities, studied philosophy and also art, and studied painting with a famous abstractionist painter.
I forget his name right now.
But Suzuki Roshi's teachings really struck her, and soon she was devoting herself full time to practice.
She was not a very flashy person.
I met her once.
I actually sat across the aisle from her at my first ever seven-day sesshin, so I have an impression of her in sesshin.
But then I just missed her.
She went on to be the head teacher, the guiding teacher of the Santa Cruz Zen Center, but she arrived there right after I left.
And oddly, I arrived right after Kobun Chino left, who was Edie's first teacher.
So I was in that particular center as a young man trying out daily Zazen and being very shy about it.
It was a center that was in between teachers, in caretaker mode for a while, for like five years or something.
Anyway, Katherine never set about to write books.
I don't know that she particularly even wrote.
She must have written newsletter essays or something, but she was not a big writer.
But like so many Zen teachers, the talks were recorded, and piles of tapes or MP3s build up somewhere.
And eventually somebody gets inspired.
This is her student Bill Annelli, with help from Natalie Goldberg.
Natalie, as you know, is a well-known Zen writer, and she was also a friend of Katherine Thanas.
Our other connection to Katherine Thanas is that when Chris went back to Santa Cruz for a couple of years to finish her career, she practiced extensively at Santa Cruz Zen Center.
Next time she's here, we can ask her for the exact chronology.
But what happened when the book was almost done, late 90s or something, early 2000s, I forget: Katherine, who was then in her 80s, slipped in the bathroom, cracked her head and never woke up again.
But she did live on in a coma with, I think, just palliative care at home, and the Zen students sat with her.
So I'm pretty sure Chris got to Santa Cruz exactly in time for that.
I don't know if she interacted with Katherine when Katherine was up and about and actively teaching or what.
But I'm pretty sure Chris got to sit with Katherine as she passed away.
So, a few excerpts from Katherine Thanas.
The first is actually setting the stage a little bit about her relationship with Suzuki Roshi, and also that she was always trying to understand her own mind, as we all are.
This is the first part of a short little chapter.
They're all short little chapters, which I think Bill and Ellie gave the names to, same as in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
This chapter is called Set Ourselves to Zero.
*We're always getting hooked by something.
For years I was hooked by the idea of perfection.
But over the years my understanding has changed.
Suzuki Roshi had taught us, nothing we see or hear is perfect.*
*But right there in the imperfection is perfect reality.
Nothing we see or hear is perfect.
But right there in the imperfection is perfect reality.
Suzuki Roshi.
But it took his Ashes Internment ceremony at Tassajara to bring this home.
Before his passing Suzuki Roshi had selected a beautiful large rock from the creek for his memorial stone.
And students had hauled it up the mountain and installed it in a quiet setting away from the sound of the creek.
The ceremony started from the former zendo, the site of the present day student eating area.*
*As the Densho bell intoned its deep voice, Baker Roshi came out of the zendo carrying Suzuki Roshi's ashes at his chest in a box wrapped in a white cloth.
The symbolism was poignant.
Suzuki Roshi had carried us for so many years.
And now his successor was carrying him in a small box.
It was a potent image, psychologically very powerful.
As sadness permeated the valley and the procession started, I noticed a young man sitting casually on the side who appeared bemused by the whole event.
The expression on his face contradicted the mood of the occasion, I thought.
I initially had imagined that his appearance and conduct detracted from the solemnity of the occasion.*
*I wanted his energy not to interfere with this ceremony.
I thought he was ruining the whole tableau.
In the midst of my thinking about what to do, unexpectedly big mind kicked in.
And a thought arose.
No, this is perfect.
Now complete.
There is both reverence, the mourning, devotional side, and also something else.
Unexpected, random, unpredictable.*
*The situation surprisingly then felt alright, and I was at ease.
This is how I learned that it is often the unexpected circumstances of our lives that help us become real.
When we first came to practice, we thought we would become like Suzuki Roshi.
If we just sat Zazen and lost our flawed personalities, that we thought we were.
But, the teaching says you practice to become yourself, not your teacher.*
That's quite a story, huh?
Can you picture that?
If you ever get to go to Tassajara, you can see that stone at the ashes site, pretty far up on the hill.
It's been quite a thing to carry that stone up there.
But we do, right?
Our mind is constantly judging, right?
Searching, seeking for things out of place, and then zeroing in on them, like that young man there.
But maybe we don't have to do that.
Maybe we really don't have to do that.
The things are okay just as they are.
So here's the main thing I want to share from her.
This is so very practical and hands-on, and I've been trying to practice with this from Katherine Thanas.
This little chapter is called No Pressure to Improve.
*Each moment arises as a world of echoes.
You're sitting with your breath, listening to thoughts, following thoughts, forgetting thoughts.
A world of echoes arises.
What would it be like to sit in Zazen and go beyond?*
*To think non-thoughts.
As soon as they arrive, they dissolve and leave no trace.
All these thoughts you've been having about your knees or your oryoki or your family, your job, worries about the future, regrets about the past.
As soon as these thoughts come up, they pass.
Nothing hooks them.
Although that's actually what's happening.
This non-thinking thing.*
*That's actually what's happening.
Habits of mind reassemble certain thoughts really quickly.
It's called reenactment.
Thoughts repeat themselves again and again.
Unless there really is no hook in the mind.
The thing about reality is that there's no later.
There's no next moment when one is going to become enlightenment.
When one is going to understand non-being, where there's no outside, no second moment, only infinite first moments arising as now.
If you recognize this as the way the universe is, everything coming and going, not belonging to anyone, that's the universe of not-self.
A sense of space.
This is the secret to Buddhist practice.
What we're studying is the mind.
Not Katherine's mind.
But the mind arising as Katherine.*
*And when Katherine can hear and accept everything that's going on in her mind, she can hear and accept everything that's going on in anybody's mind.
Nothing is outside her mind.
In that mind, there is no pressure to improve Katherine.
It is, quote, to be without anxiety about non-perfection.
As Senkan, the second ancestor, says.
From that place, there's no anxiety about right or wrong, and yet there is complete understanding of causes and conditions.*
*Someone said recently, she's noticed that when she comes close to something important, she veers off.
This is an important awareness.
What does it take to go straight ahead?
To notice the moments when we veer off.
How much effort is enough?
What's too hard?
Our life can be measured in moments of backing off or going straight ahead.
Backing off of conflict, difficulty, frustration, fear, or a willingness to trust and go with the moment.*
*Not because it's comfortable, but because it's there.
It's here.
When we're most completely ourselves, we're most completely free of ourselves.
But you can't think about it.
You have to completely be the complicated, mysterious being that each of it is and is embarrassed by.
Is there anyone here is not embarrassed by the completely enigmatic, mysterious being that you are?*
We could ask that here.
Is anybody not embarrassed by yourself a little bit?
*As long as we're embarrassed, there's a self there.
There's a defense.
There's some resistance.
How about being willing to be embarrassed, to be resilient, or to be either?
Either way.
Stop veering off.
You have to go into it.
You take a little step toward it and take another little step.*
*You go as slowly as you need to.
You come right in and put your nose down close to it.
Maybe you don't want to get that close.
You can only do what your stomach can do.
So you do it slowly, at the pace at which your stomach and heart can handle it.
When we get really tight and solid, so does the energy of fear.
If you become relaxed and just sit there with fear, inhaling and exhaling, fear is going to relax too.
It might change shape.
It might get smaller or larger.
But it's never going to be bigger than you because it's your energy.
Fear is never greater than our body.
So what we have to do when our heart is ready, when our minds and stomach are ready, is to get up close inside it.
Breathe it.
Smell it.
Mind has to bring fear back inside the body because it's the mind that has put fear outside.
It's the mind that says, I am not going to acknowledge that fear or work with it.
It's too much.
So you allow your consciousness to experience the sensation and you stay with it.
You don't go somewhere else in your mind and wish it would go away.
You enter the experience with an inhalation and with an exhalation.
You feel the coldness, the movement, the solidity or the dissolution with a quiet, steady mind.*
I'm just going to reread the last couple of paragraphs there.
This is what I was really wanting to point to.
It's very powerful, very specific advice.
Like really getting under the hood of the mind here, huh?
The first thing to highlight is this interesting point about being embarrassed.
We were so used to being a little embarrassed by ourselves, we stopped even noticing it.
When we're embarrassed, there's some self holding on, right?
Somehow holding on.
So what are we holding on to?
And then we have this great thing from her: stop veering off.
*You have to go into it.
You take a little step toward it.
You take another little step.
You go as slowly as you need to.
You might come right in and put your nose down close to it.
Maybe you don't want to get that close yet.
You can only do what your stomach can do.
So you do it slowly at the pace at which your stomach and your heart can handle it.
When we get really tight and solid, so does the energy of fear.
If you become relaxed and just sit there with the fear, inhaling and exhaling, fear is going to relax too.
It might change shape.
It might get smaller or bigger.
But it's never going to be bigger than you because it's your energy.
Fear is never greater than our body.
So what we have to do when our heart is ready and our mind and stomach are ready is to get up close, inside it, breathe it, smell it.
And mind has to bring fear back into our body because it's the mind that put fear outside.
It's the mind that says, I'm not going to acknowledge that fear or work with it.
You allow your consciousness to experience the sensation and you stay with it.
You don't go somewhere else in your mind and wish you would go away.
You enter the experience with an inhalation and an exhalation.
You feel the coldness, the movement, the solidity, or the dissolution with a quiet, steady mind.*
Great practice advice there, huh?
Also, it's worth noticing she doesn't say what you get out of all that.
She makes no promises, which is good.
And this felt fortuitous to me because lately my experience, when the mind is tight, is that I'm starting to really notice there's a lot of fear.
There's a lot of fear.
I've always known at some level that there's fear, deep down there somewhere.
I remember times in sesshin and during...

Actually, I have some particular memories from Tassajara, where I felt like I could feel this dark, cold kind of stone, deep down in my gut, below my gut somewhere, somewhere that wasn't exactly physical but was.
This really intense, cold, dark place.
Somehow, when I was curious about what it was, what came back was that it was fear.
I got some help from teachers working with that.
But down there somewhere, not bothering me up here, when I get quiet enough: ooh, look at that.
But lately it seems like the fear is ready to express itself more.
I wonder if you're having that experience too.
One of the ways I've been trying to practice with it, and I had a really strong experience with this a couple of mornings ago, was just to try to name it.
This is fear.
This is the feeling of fear.
And try to turn down the stories that it attaches to, which I think is what she means by the mind needing to bring the fear back inside the body, because the mind put the fear outside the body.
So outside the body, our fear, our shame, our embarrassment, our anger, whatever it is, it attaches to things, right?
It attaches to stories.
In my case, most often the story is that I must have upset somebody.
You show a particular person, not just generic.
My mind gets busy looking for evidence that I must have upset such and so, and I feel fearful that they're upset with me, mad at me, don't like me anymore or something.
I notice the mind is really good at finding that evidence when I'm in that state, kind of like what the scientists call confirmation bias.
But it's just a story.
It's not true.
Sometimes somebody is upset with me and I don't even know.
I can't be fearful of that because I don't even know what's happening.
But the fear is so different from the stories of what's happening, it seems.
When I can breathe with it and be with it, not veer off like she says, it's a lot more possible to see fear as fear and just be there with it.
Wow.
Breathe with it, sit with it, walk with it.
But it doesn't have to ruin my day exactly either.
These are powerful things, I do know that.
So I wonder how it is for each of you, each of us.
But such great, specific advice from Katherine Thanas, right?
Stop veering off.
Go into it.
Step into it.
Take a little step.
But also compassionate, kind and gentle.
Go as slowly as you need to.
Feel into how your stomach's doing.
Is your stomach still soft or is it in knots?
What is your heart up for?
What's the pace?
And Suzuki Roshi's words, enigmatic is probably the best word, do give some feeling for this territory.
A powerful feeling for this territory, actually an amazing feeling for this territory.
But not how to operate or how to move around.
Right?
He's just giving us a big meadow, like his wonderful metaphor of giving a cow a big meadow for us to wander around and find our way.
But what a blessing also to have teachers who can say to other teachers, well, you might look over there.
I think there might be something there to look at for you.
See what you see.
Which is still not telling us what to do, how to fix anything.
I love that about that little passage from Katherine Thanas.
She gives us a lot of things to do, but not why, or not what it's going to lead to exactly.
But here's a way to practice.
Here's a way to investigate.
And so beautiful and important to be reminded again and again that all this is happening in the body.
Right?
Our heads and our stories so dominate.
I notice when I'm hanging out with the fear and it's really strong, I can feel the movement of the breathing, but I can't really feel the sensations in the body as well.
I don't notice the absence, but I can't.
What I do notice is, when the fear releases, such a fuller feeling in the body.
Yeah, the belly, the stomach gets soft.
There's a feeling of circulation of energy in the torso, which seems to go clockwise for some reason.
And I've got various experiences and stories about different aspects of me that seem to be somewhere in that system.
Good teachers and therapists and crises, you know.
So we learn from our body and our body learns with us.
But we do need our intentionality.
So, like she says, using our mind to bring it back into the body.
Bring it back into the body.
But of course, another huge part of all this, which is more Suzuki Roshi's emphasis, is that we don't actually have to do anything at all, because everything changes.
All this stuff is so impermanent and empty.
One day, an eruption of fear.
Next day or next moment, ease and joy.
This does happen.
We don't know if it'll happen or when it'll happen.
It doesn't work that way.
We can't be in a miserable state and tell ourselves, okay, how long will it be till it gets better?
Right?
That doesn't seem to help at all.
But we stay with it.
Don't veer off.
It does change.
And I don't know if we had anything to do with that change or not.
Everything changes without our needing to change it.
Moods are so powerful and ideas are so powerful and projections onto ourselves and others in our world are so powerful because we believe them.
But moods and ideas and projections and theories are also empty, right?
They're also transitory.
Sometimes you get new information and your theory just collapses.
Other times you bat the new information away and cling to your theory.
But none of it's real in the way that we think it is either, is it?
And yet it is.
And I do know that some mental phenomena are of a whole other order of intensity.
It may be a lifetime before they change, like clinical depression.
So there are no simple answers in any of this.
No simple solutions.
And yet we can also watch out for not telling ourselves simple stories about how locked in we are to any of this either, right?
The story of my problem, the story of my limitations.
And of course, the huge emphasis from Suzuki Roshi is just zazen, sitting in the middle of it all.
The way zazen done over years and decades broadens our perspective.
We can't help it.
It's just organic.

It broadens our patience, makes us more resilient and able to hang out through the volatility and the allowing of life to throw through us and change, and even when things are horrible, to really hang in there.
So I want to bring Katherine Thanas, Suzuki Roshi's disciple, in.
Thank you, Katherine Thanas Roshi.
Let's talk a little bit about difficult emotions.
I know we're all different in that regard.
We did breakout rooms last week, so maybe we won't do breakout rooms this week.
We could just reflect on our own.
How is it for you when strong emotional states and strong inner mental experience just takes hold, just grabs hold of you?
How do you meet that and how can you practice with that?
Are there ways that you could drop out of the story?
Are there ways that you could bring it into the body?
And what are the dominant difficult emotional states or mental states for you?

I remember at one point, and I keep getting to early days because of all these Suzuki Roshi stories and Tassajara and stuff, but I remember once when I was at Green Gulch or City Center or somewhere, there were all these discussions about using the three poisons: greed, hatred, and delusion.
It's kind of like this simplistic personality typing.
So are you a greed person, a hatred person, or a delusion person?
That's another way to look at it.
We're more complicated than that, but that's a useful frame.
And of course we're a little embarrassed by all this because we have that stickiness of self.
Greed, hatred, and delusion.
Do you tend to be greedy?
And greedy doesn't mean you're stealing money or something, necessarily.
It's where the mind emphasizes desire a lot.
And it's okay.
It's natural, right?
It's conditioned.
So we need to be honest with ourselves.
Does the mind often want things?
Want things to be a certain way, not another way?
Maybe you're a greed type.
Hatred is also anger.
Does the mind tend towards anger, reactivity, intensity, actual hatred?
Do you rage inside?
Or delusion?
Do you tend towards confusion and delusion?
I always put myself in that last one.
Put myself down as the delusion type.
I hardly even seem to know how to get angry.
I'm not good at anger or hatred.
I'm getting a little better.
We had some good work in the sangha around that that helped me.
I don't think I'm too big of a greed type, but of course there's always some.
I'm often generous.
But boy, I get so tangled up so easily that when there's any pressure or anything confusing, or especially interpersonal tension, I freeze.
So I just want to invite all of us to reflect on this and think about whether these teachings are helpful to you.
And this balancing of form and emptiness is so important here.
In a way, there's nothing to do.
Just keep practicing.
In a way, it's good to have some direction, some intentionality, some purposefulness.
How am I practicing for myself and for all beings so that I can be a more useful Bodhisattva in this world?
Thank you very much.
